# The additional question repeated visits can answer

The GBIF-only model asks where ecological intensity is relatively high after
accounting for a named recording-bias covariate.  A designed survey adds a
different kind of information: repeated visits at the same cell can distinguish
failure to observe a species from low ecological occurrence opportunity.  That
is the reason to add replicated surveys.  It is not a reason to add a generic
zero-inflation component to every rare-species model.

This article specifies the planned integrated joint species distribution model
(iJSDM).  It is local-only staging material.  The repeated-visit detection
likelihood, its synthetic generator, and its known-truth recovery campaign are
not yet implemented; readers must not treat the equations below as an
available package workflow.

# Shared ecology, source-specific observation

The ecological state stays exactly the same as in the first article:

\[
  \eta_{cs}=\alpha_s+x_c^\top\beta_s+\lambda_s z_c+e_{cs},\qquad
  \operatorname{Var}(\eta_c\mid x_c)=\Lambda\Lambda^\top+\Psi.
\]

Opportunistic records retain their source-specific Poisson observation law:

\[
  N^G_{cs}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}\left[
  a^G_c\exp\{\eta_{cs}+b_c\gamma_s\}\right].
\]

For a scheduled survey at visit \(v\), define the ecological occurrence
probability induced by intensity and known survey support,

\[
  q_{csv}=1-\exp\left[-a^S_{cv}\exp(\eta_{cs})\right].
\]

Let the conditional detection probability be

\[
  p_{csv}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(w_{cv}^\top\delta_s),
\]

where \(w_{cv}\) contains visit conditions such as observer effort, date, or
weather.  The planned observed detection model is

\[
  Y_{csv}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\{p_{csv}q_{csv}\}.
\]

The three channels are conditionally independent given \(\eta_{cs}\) and the
source/visit covariates.  Each channel therefore informs the same ecology but
has its own observation mechanism.

# Why this is not ordinary zero inflation

The product \(p_{csv}q_{csv}\) has a scientific interpretation.  A zero can
occur because the ecological event did not occur over the survey support
(\(q_{csv}\)), or because the event occurred but the survey missed it
(\(p_{csv}\)).  Repeated visits with changing detection covariates provide the
replication that can separate those explanations.  An unconstrained extra-zero
mixture would not automatically have that interpretation and can be confounded
with low \(\eta_{cs}\), especially for rare species.

The planned identification design has three non-negotiable parts.  First,
there are repeated visits at the same cells.  Second, at least one detection
covariate varies by visit rather than only by cell.  Third, ecological and
detection covariates are not aliases of each other in the synthetic design.
The known-truth campaign must demonstrate recovery of \(\beta_s\),
\(\gamma_s\), \(\delta_s\), the ecological maps, and the covariance
decomposition before this becomes a public workflow.

# What the eventual synthetic workflow will show

The final worked example will use a restoration-monitoring landscape with six
wetland species, a GBIF-like opportunistic-record channel, and three planned
survey visits.  It will show the data in long form and the corresponding wide
form through `gllvmTMB()` only after the public interface exists.  It will
report relative ecological intensity—not abundance—and will visibly separate
ecological covariates, GBIF-bias covariates, and visit-level detection
covariates.

The core simulation will deliberately include rare species and many zeros.
Its diagnostic question is not whether a penalty forces a nonzero estimate.  It
is whether the repeated-visit design recovers detection and ecology separately
when the truth is known.  Failure would be useful evidence: it would narrow
the identifiable regime instead of being hidden by a generic zero-inflation
term.

# Boundaries before spatial structure

Neither article currently includes spatial autocorrelation.  Adding a spatial
ecological field and a separate GBIF-bias field raises a new confounding
problem: both can explain geographical clustering in opportunistic records.
That is a dedicated later arc.  It will use the package's mesh-based SPDE/GMRF
representation—sparse mesh basis weights and a sparse precision matrix—not a
dense coordinate covariance matrix.  First, the nonspatial
ecological-plus-detection model must recover known truth.  Only then should
mesh-based controls such as a shared `latent()` term plus
`spatial_indep(common = TRUE)`, and a compact
`spatial_latent(..., unique = TRUE)` alternative, be compared against known
two-field truths.

# References to verify before promotion

Before public promotion, add verified citations for repeated-visit occupancy
and detection models, integrated species-distribution models, and multivariate
latent-factor JSDMs.  The article must also link to a successful private
known-truth recovery record and a runnable synthetic public API example.
